hero.name: Adidev Panday
hero.intro: I'm a Woodstock School student from Ludhiana, India, headed for aerospace engineering. I build AI-driven apps, publish research, and spend my spare hours watching my interesting Youtube feed, F1, playing the violin, and playing sports. Below, you will find everything that I'm proud of.

about.heading: About Me
paragraphs: I grew up in Ludhiana, Punjab, and study at Woodstock School, taking HL Physics, Math AA, and Computer Science in the IB Diploma. My focus is aerospace engineering where I hope to learn about aerodynamics & propulsion.

Outside class, I love building things. I've shipped many AI-powered web apps, developed a React Native app to tackle teen drunk-driving in my hometown, and published research on the risks of digital trading. I co-founded my school's AI Club, lead the yearbook as Editor in Chief, and used to play first chair violin in the Advanced Orchestra. I've competed in varsity football and basketball, interned in product development and CAD, and served on the Academic Honesty Council (AHC) & NHS.

Personally I feel drawn to problems that reward not just rigor but also creativity: from modeling 4th-down football decisions with game theory for my Extended Essay to studying how a paper plane's wing generates lift for my IA.

research.title: The Rise of Digital Trading: Accessibility Versus Risk of Financial Ruin
research.journal: International Journal of High School Research (IJHSR), Vol. 8, Issue 12
research.pageNote: Paper begins on page 89 of the issue.
research.abstract: Digital trading platforms like Robinhood, Groww, and Zerodha have made market access a few clicks away for anyone, educated or not. This paper examines that double-edged shift, covering gamification, finfluencers, and the real cost of frictionless trading. Digitization is useful, but for financially illiterate users, it is a trapdoor.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to the IJHSR issue PDF. My paper starts on page 89.

research.title: F1 CAR ON A CEILING?
research.abstract: Four documentaries claim an F1 car could drive upside down in a tunnel. None say how fast. This paper builds a ground-effect model of a 2022 to 2025 car and shows the honest answer is not a speed but a window, from 208 km/h where the car can finally hold its own motion, up to 327 km/h where its floor gets dragged into the ceiling.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to f1onceiling.netlify.app, an interactive version of the paper.

whyAerospace.heading: Why Aerospace?
whyAerospace.subtitle: F1; My Childhood Love
paragraphs: I was three years old in a red toy Formula 1 car before I knew what a car really was, and I have been chasing the same feeling ever since. F1 introduced me to physics: that races are won and lost in how air bends around a machine, that a wing is just an upside-down piece of metal, that seconds are gained and lost through millimeters. This obsession with aerodynamics grew up alongside me.

But aerodynamics is not the full story. Propulsion is what actually currently attracts me to it, ironic right? Thrust perplexes me: how you take stored energy and turn it into controlled, enormous force, how a column of plasma or a breath of burning air can move a body through a sky or past an atmosphere. I think aerodynamics is how a machine survives the unforgiving air but propulsion is how it refuses to be affected by it. That is why I love aerospace.

defaultTemplate.opener: I am applying to {school} because its program lines up with where I want to take my aerospace work.
bullets: Add the most specific course, lab, or professor at {school} that matches propulsion, aerodynamics, or aerospace.
Add the most specific student team, facility, or project at {school} worth naming.
Add the personal fit reason, grounded in something already built or done.
MAE 426. Jet theory, combustion control, scramjets. Things I would study in my free time out of my own free will.
Dr. Choueiri's EPPDyL by sophomore year. Hall thrusters, plasma instabilities, the quiet end of propulsion.
Team Orbital, 2027 TigerCub launch. I want my face on princetonrocketry.com/members, standing next to Talon Flores (MAE '28) when the thing goes up.
princeton.pullQuote: Rocket-physics and violin-physics are somehow the same physics.
princeton.closing: Nine and a half time zones ahead. Still awake.

bullets: AAE 439. Combustion instability, why pressure oscillations couple with the acoustic modes of the hardware, why an engine tears itself apart or doesn't.
Zucrow test cell, LOX/methane, 124 seconds of Morpheus hotfire, Mach diamonds in the plume. I've watched the video 14 times.
I want to be in that cell by sophomore year. The kid nobody trusts with the good welds yet, learning by holding things and breaking a few.
purdue.pullQuote: Shock waves repeating in a pattern I can almost, but not quite, derive.
purdue.closing: 14 replays in. I want to make the next video, not just watch it.

uiuc.opener: The ISS Hybrid team is why.
bullets: AE 433 and AE 434. Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, nozzle expansion ratios, specific impulse, and the combustion coupling that decides whether a chamber survives.
Illinois Space Society Hybrid, hot-firing at Willard airport's retired jet-engine testing facility. 20 students, 8 years, one engine.
I've watched that hotfire 11 times already. I want to graduate knowing how to build the next one, not rewatch it a twelfth.
uiuc.pullQuote: 4 kilonewtons of thrust. Nytrox and paraffin. A chamber students built across eight years.
uiuc.closing: Four years from now, knowing how to design what I'd been rewatching.

bullets: AOE 4234 and AOE 4604. Propulsion systems one semester, booster design, fabrication, and operation the next.
PropEL's hypersonic wind tunnel. Mach 2 through 7, steady flow for 15 seconds, run after run.
I built airflowns.netlify.app to solve 2D Navier-Stokes in a browser. That's incompressible subsonic. PropEL runs compressible hypersonic. Same equations, different regime, no laptop can touch it.
virginia-tech.pullQuote: 15 seconds of steady flow my laptop will never simulate.

georgia-tech.opener: Both ends of propulsion. Same campus.
bullets: AE 4451. Jet and rocket propulsion in one course.
Ben T. Zinn Combustion Lab for the chemical side. HPEPL's vacuum chamber for Hall thrusters on the electric side. Both at walking distance.
I haven't decided between chemical and electric propulsion yet, and I'd rather not have to at 18. GT lets me take both before I commit.
georgia-tech.pullQuote: I don't want to pick chemical or electric at 18.

bullets: S.B. Mechanical Engineering at SEAS. Fluid mechanics, continuum, vorticity. The equations I first met taping wings onto paper planes.
Harvard Undergraduate Aerospace Collective. First Crimson CubeSat. Mojave Sphinx, the Ivy League's first student liquid bi-propellant rocket.
Harvard doesn't name an aerospace degree, which means I get to build the path. Government and Economics on the same transcript as fluids is how I already think.
16.50, then 16.512. Aerospace propulsion, then chemical and liquid-bipropellant rocket propulsion.
MIT Rocket Team, Space Propulsion Lab, Draper Lab two blocks away for a UROP.
Reach. I know. But AirflowNS, a published IJHSR paper, and 14 replays of a Purdue hotfire mean I'd show up for the work, not the brand on the sweatshirt.

uc-berkeley.opener: A new major at an old powerhouse.
bullets: Aerospace Engineering, the major Berkeley launched in 2025, built on top of 150 years of mechanical engineering.
Space Technologies at Cal (STAC) for CubeSats and attitude control. New program, room to help decide what it becomes.
I'd rather help shape a two-year-old major at a real engineering school than slot into a program that's already decided what it is.

uc-davis.opener: A UC that calls it aerospace.
bullets: EAE 130A and 130B. Two quarters of aerospace vehicle design.
The department's own aeronautical wind tunnel, plus UC Davis's reputation in aeroacoustics and unsteady flows.
"Aerospace Science and Engineering" as the actual degree name, not "mechanical with a track." The name tells me where the department puts its attention.
MAE 150. Gas turbines, ramjets, scramjets, rotating detonation engines in one course.
UCI Combustion Laboratory. Smaller than Zucrow or Zinn Lab. Also one of the most-cited combustion groups in the country.
Rotating detonation engines are the next generation of propulsion. UCI is already running them.

uc-san-diego.opener: Number one public MAE by citations.
bullets: MAE 101A, 101B, 101C. Fluid mechanics, viscous flows, compressible flows. The full ladder.
UCSD's hypersonics group and their CFD lab. Deep on flow control and transition.
My F1-on-a-ceiling paper lives in ground effect. UCSD works at Mach 10 plus. Same equations, next regime up.
MAE 157A rocket propulsion. MAE 157B electric propulsion. Both offered. Both get taken.
Dr. Richard Wirz's Plasma and Space Propulsion Laboratory. Hall thrusters, hollow cathodes.
Chemical propulsion is loud. Plasma is where the next decade of deep-space thrust actually lives. UCLA takes plasma seriously.
MEng Aerospace Engineering with a full year in industry. Not an internship. A proper year.
Core mechanical engineering in the first two years. Aerodynamics and propulsion later, after I've earned it.
I've done two months of CAD at BAUM. A full year on an engineering floor before graduation is the next step I actually want.

bristol.opener: Aero in the town that built the Concorde.
bullets: MEng Aerospace Engineering with the National Composites Centre on campus.
Filton is 15 minutes away. Airbus, Rolls-Royce, GKN, the last Concorde ever flown, all in that one postcode.
Studying aerospace in the town where the Concorde was designed is not a small thing.

manchester.opener: Reynolds did his pipe experiment here.
bullets: MEng Aerospace Engineering. Osborne Reynolds ran his pipe experiment in this university in 1883.
Every Reynolds number I've calculated for a Physics IA started in this building.
When the number is named after someone whose desk was here, the equation stops feeling abstract.
The Melbourne Model. A Bachelor of Science first, then a Master of Engineering (Aerospace).
Dr. Ivan Marusic's Fluid Mechanics Group. World-class on turbulent boundary layers, the exact regime I want to understand.
I'm a violinist who builds AI apps and publishes research. Melbourne is one of the few universities that doesn't ask me to pick just one of those first.
AEROSP 320 for propulsion, AEROSP 325 for gas dynamics.
Dr. Alec Gallimore's PEPL. The X3 Hall thruster: 100+ kilowatts, built with NASA, aimed at a crewed Mars mission.
Michigan builds the thruster NASA will actually use. Not a scale model. The thruster.
MEng Aerospace Engineering, with the AMRC (Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre) on campus, built in partnership with Boeing.
CAD at BAUM taught me design. Sheffield's next step is machining, composites, and layup.
Design is half of being an engineer. Sheffield teaches the half most courses skip on the way to a theory exam.

southampton.opener: Mitchell's tunnel. F1 teams rent it.
bullets: R.J. Mitchell Wind Tunnel. Mitchell designed the Spitfire. Current F1 teams pay to use that tunnel.
The only Russell Group MEng that puts Aeronautics AND Astronautics in the same degree. Air and space, with a vacuum chamber on site.
Downforce pulled me in. Thrust kept me. Southampton tests both in the same building.
BSc in Mathematical and Computing Sciences for Artificial Intelligence. One rigorous subject, taught as a single discipline.
Milan. A city that runs on finance and design, with a working job market for the AI I'd study.
I've built five AI apps and published research on digital trading in IJHSR. Bocconi is where those two stop being hobbies.

hku-berkeley.opener: A degree built out of two places.
bullets: Two years at HKU for mechanical engineering, two years at Berkeley for the new aerospace major.
HKU is one of Asia's top MechE departments. Berkeley just launched aerospace. The pairing isn't coincidence, it's by design.
I grew up in Ludhiana and study at Woodstock. A degree built across two institutions is the version I'd pick on paper too.

nus.opener: I've already been on that campus.
bullets: The Aerospace Engineering specialisation inside NUS Mechanical Engineering. QS #8 globally for engineering.
I spent a week at NUS Science Summer Camp in 2025. Prof. Sow Chorng Haur's nanotech lecture is still the clearest explanation of quantum confinement I've heard.
Asia's fastest-moving research funding, 5 hours from Ludhiana. Studying aerospace in the region I'm actually from.

tu-delft.opener: Walk into the tunnel. Watch it hold.
bullets: The full BSc in the only Faculty of Aerospace Engineering in the Netherlands. QS #4 globally for aerospace.
Subsonic, supersonic, and hypersonic tunnels past Mach 11. A Cessna they use as a classroom. A clean room where students build satellites.
I derived the lift equation in a Math HL IA. Delft is where I'd walk into the tunnel and watch the math hold.

tum.opener: Classroom to test stand. Very short walk.
bullets: The Chair of Turbomachinery and Flight Propulsion (LRG) in Ottobrunn. Turbines, engines, fuel-to-thrust.
Airbus Defence and Space, and MTU, a few minutes down the road from the lecture hall.
Germany's top aerospace program, planted inside Germany's aerospace cluster. The gap between a lecture and a real test stand is unusually short.
